articles.title: Maybe I’m Just Not Meant to Make Money (Reflections on Building a Product)
articles.excerpt: I opened Google Analytics to check the traffic to a website I’d been working on. Here’s what I saw: Active users: 0. New users: 0. Average engagement time: 0 seconds. Event count: 0. Four zeros. I sta…
articles.body: I opened Google Analytics to check the traffic to a website I’d been working on. Here’s what I saw: Active users: 0. New users: 0. Average engagement time: 0 seconds. Event count: 0. Four zeros. I stared at the screen for a while. There was nothing technically wrong with the dashboard. It was simply showing me what had happened. And somehow, that felt worse, because behind those zeros were many hours of work that the dashboard knew absolutely nothing about. The Website Nobody Asked Me to Build A few weeks earlier, I had started building a website called CutDone. Most productivity apps help people add tasks, organize them, and track them. I wanted to build something that helped people make tasks disappear.

articles.body: I built a sloth that cleans my Downloads folder — meet slothsort 🦥 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3 — Slow and Steady. What I built slothsort is a small Python CLI that tidies a messy folder for you. Point it at your Downloads directory — you know the one, with Q3-budget-final-FINAL.xlsx living next to screenshot 2026-10-19.png and an installer from 2024 — and it sorts everything into tidy category folders: Documents, Images, Videos, Audio, Archives, Installers, Code, and friends. The twist: the sorting decisions are made by Gemma, running locally through Ollama . No accounts, no API keys, no filenames leaving your machine.

articles.title: I stopped blaming GPT-5 for my Ads API 401 OAuth mess and fixed the 4 auth states that were actually broken
articles.excerpt: I lost a stupid amount of time blaming GPT-5 for an automation failure that had nothing to do with GPT-5. The setup looked normal enough: n8n pulls search term data from Google Ads GPT-5 classifies wa…
articles.body: I lost a stupid amount of time blaming GPT-5 for an automation failure that had nothing to do with GPT-5. The setup looked normal enough: n8n pulls search term data from Google Ads GPT-5 classifies waste vs opportunity a review step approves changes the workflow pushes budget updates back Instead, the job kept dying around 2 a.m. with a 401. Then a Make scenario started failing on a Meta sync. Then a Python worker started returning invalid_grant . Then I did what a lot of us do when an "AI workflow" breaks: I blamed the model layer. Maybe GPT-5 was acting weird. Maybe Claude had generated a bad payload. Maybe the prompt had drifted. Maybe my routing logic was flaky. Nope. The real problem was much more boring: auth.

articles.title: Why I cap daily invites at 3 (and what happens when I change it)
articles.excerpt: For my WebDAV mount tool (ScsDriver, $5.50 lifetime), I built a 7-day free trial that can be extended to 60+ days via a referral system. The single most important design decision was the daily invite…
articles.body: For my WebDAV mount tool (ScsDriver, $5.50 lifetime), I built a 7-day free trial that can be extended to 60+ days via a referral system. The single most important design decision was the daily invite cap. Here's the long-form comparison after running both unlimited and capped variants for the past 8 months. What changed In v1.0 (Q1 2025), I shipped unlimited invites. "Unlimited" meant: send as many referrals as you want, get +14 days for each accepted one. In v2.0 (Q2 2025), I capped it at 5 per day. In v3.0 (Q3 2025), I dropped the cap to 3 per day. What I expected I expected lowering the cap to reduce spam behavior. I expected it to also reduce legitimate user activity (since power users would hit the cap). What actually happened with cap=5 Referral volume dropped 30% in the first week.

articles.excerpt: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli arrived at Mars! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars ! ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars , and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground. Schiaparelli did not survive the accident , but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity.

articles.title: The moon is shrinking. 10,000 cracks on the lunar surface reveal by how much
articles.excerpt: One new study shows how much the moon has diminished over time.
articles.body: The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years. The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process . Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting. In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
